new_statements.quote: There are a few general rules that govern the pronunciation of these forms. i) Primary stress always fall on the first syllable of a word. [p. 27] ... The first stress rule places heavy stress on the first syllable of every word and on the first syllable of the second member of a compound word, hence it applies iteratively to as many segments as meet the structural conditions for its application. The second rule reduces the stress on the second element of a compound word. (Primary stress is indicated by means of the symbol /´/, secondary stress by means of /˝/.) P.R.1. Stress Placement (SP) ... P.R.2. Stress Reduction (SR) [p. 124]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. p. 4 (printed page number 27 visible on the render) reads verbatim: "There are a few general rules that govern the pronunciation of these forms. i) Primary stress always fall on the first syllable of a word. ii) A syllable break is normally made before the last consonant of a consonant sequence.." The second part of the report's quote ("The first stress rule places heavy stress on the first syllable of every word and on the first syllable of the second member of a compound word, hence it applies iteratively.. The second rule reduces the stress on the second element of a compound word. (Primary stress is indicated by means of the symbol.. secondary stress by…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word, without exception; in compounds each member keeps first-syllable stress but the second member is reduced to secondary stress. Stress is predictable (rule-assigned), not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only in compounds: the first syllable of the second (head) element carries secondary stress, stronger than other non-initial syllables (p. 37 fn. 16, p. 124 P.R.2). No rhythmic secondary stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: None for simple words ('always'). Compounds: first element's first syllable takes major stress, the head noun (second element) takes secondary stress (p. 37 fn. 16; p. 38; P.R.2 p. 124). Bound feminine classifier ha:ri: after kinship terms is weakly stressed (p. 37 fn. 16). Words with underlying long consonants show a very short stressed first syllable followed by a long second syllable (p. 33 fn. 11).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'the first syllable of a word'; the rule is stated for the pronunciation of stem forms and then formalized as P.R.1 applying to every phonological word and to each member of a compound (with the second member reduced to secondary stress by P.R.2). Stress is treated as non-contrastive and rule-assigned; vowel length is contrastive only in initial syllables (p. 27-28). Confidence is 'low' for east2340 only because the described variety is Western Muria, not Eastern Muria (see the note on which variety); as a statement about Sonapal Muria it is unambiguous.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is NOT about Eastern Muria. Andres 1977 describes the Muria Gondi of Sonapal village, Narayanpur Tahsil (intro p. 1), which Beine 1994/2013 p. 47 lists as test point mso in the WESTERN Muria group (Appendix A p. 96: 'Muria from Narayanpur Tehsil'); Beine's Eastern Muria (p. 49) = Lanjoda, Kondagaon Tehsil (mlj) and Raigarh, Umerkote Tehsil, Koraput/Nabarangpur, Odisha (gok), with only 69-73% intelligibility between the two groups. Glottolog itself files Andres (as 1978) under west2408 Western Muria [mut], which is a separate target in our source list (scan classification the named source could not be reached; the thesis is now obtained by the project under east2340/ and can be reused there). Andres also notes (intro p. 5) that over half of Sonapal's residents descend from Abujhmarh Marias, so 'Muria Gondi' may be a misnomer even for her variety. The Far Western Muria statement (Mathew & Mathew 2013) belongs to farw1235 [fmu]. No first-hand description of Eastern Muria proper (east2340) was found.

I Phonology p. 27: 'Primary stress always fall on the first syllable of a word'; p. 37 fn. 16: in compounds the first element's first syllable takes stronger stress than the second element's, whose first syllable is still stronger than other non-initial syllables; p. 124 P.R.1 Stress Placement puts heavy stress on the first syllable of every word and of the second member of a compound, P.R.2 reduces the compound's second element to secondary stress. sources.note: SISTER variety farw1235 [fmu] (Kurkheda tehsil, Gadchiroli, Maharashtra), not Eastern Muria. Sec. 2.4 pp. 6-7: 'In general, words carry primary stress on the first syllable.. in some sentence frames and for some phonological word types primary stress is carried by the final syllable'; sec. 9 pp. 67-68: 'Stress is not contrastive in Far Western Muria. Stress is phonetically realized by loudness, a rise in pitch and a slight lengthening of the vowel of the stressed syllable'; words with short V1 and tap/flap onset of syllable 2 get final stress with V1 reduction (uṛm 'louse', taras 'snake').

The only Muria thesis on Shodhganga is Andres 1977 (two records, hdl 10603/563349 Vol. I and 10603/149218 Vol. II). Other Gondi theses found are for Adilabad Gondi, Parsi Gondi of Mandla/Balaghat/Betul, Abujhmaria, Dandami Maria, Vidarbha Gondi — none Eastern Muria. No Muria phonology article in Crossref/OpenAlex.
Phoneme tables only, sourced from Mathew & Mathew 2013 (Far Western Muria); nothing on stress; no other Muria description cited.
